title: Long Way brand audit, moodboards, and logo exploration
goal: Do a market research analysis and first concepts for a brand
context: I'm a freelance brand and graphic designer, and a full rebrand is the largest and most common type of project I take on. This one is for Long Way, a Mar del Plata-based handmade jackets company. Their current identity was put together ad hoc years ago and didn’t hold up through the years. A rebrand means working out what the company should stand for, exploring several visual directions, choosing one, building a complete system of logo + typography + color, testing that system on real objects (packaging, signage, social posts), and finally writing it all up in a brand guidelines document so that anyone else (a printer, a web developer, the client's own marketing person) can apply the brand correctly without me in the room. Each step depends on the outputs of the previous one, and the process is not strictly linear: Step 6 is a critique round that deliberately sends me back into Steps 2–3 before I can move on. The final deliverables are a 30-page brand guidelines PDF and a packaged asset kit handed off to the client.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: I was able to complete my goal because Claude gave me thorough responses that helped me move forward faster.

Step 1.step_action: Upload the client's existing brand assets and their filled-in questionnaire and ask Claude to audit what is working and what is failing in the current identity. Ask it to research five competitors' positioning and visual language and build a comparison matrix, then draft a creative brief with objective, audience, tone and mandatories. I then rewrite the brief in my own words and lock the strategic direction.

nodes.label: State project goal on camera
nodes.detail: The user narrates that they will analyze Long Way, an Argentine handmade water-resistant jacket brand around 40-45 years old with no online presence. They outline today's plan: brand audit, competitor analysis, moodboards, choice of visual direction, and a critique round with Claude.

nodes.label: Upload brand assets and send audit prompt
nodes.detail: In the Claude desktop app they upload Long_Way_Client_Questionnaire.pdf, Long_Way_Client_Brief.pdf, and the client's existing logo image, noting the brand has nothing else to work from. They send a prompt asking Claude to do a brand audit, research five competitors' positioning/visual language/e-commerce, build a comparison matrix, and draft a creative brief with audience, objective, tone and mandatories.

nodes.label: Read uploads and ask clarifying questions
nodes.detail: Claude reads the two PDFs to ground the audit in what the client actually said, then asks three clarifying questions: which competitor set to research (Mixed AR+global / Argentina only / International only), what deliverable format is wanted, and how deep the audit should go on Long Way's own brand (including a logo critique).

nodes.label: Answer clarifying questions
nodes.detail: The user selects Argentina-only competitors since the brand doesn't compete internationally, requests two PDFs as deliverables, and asks Claude to include a logo critique alongside the audit.

nodes.label: Research competitors and render audit plus creative brief
nodes.detail: Claude searches the web and surfaces Centomo, an unexpected strong local competitor and Mar del Plata jacket maker since 1985 that explicitly states it does no online sales ('No hacemos ventas online ni envios'). It finalizes a five-brand competitive set (Ansilta, Montagne, Cardon, Ombu, Centomo), flags that the client's existing logo works against the brief (surf/skate visual language), and renders both a Brand & Competitive Audit and a Creative Brief as formatted PDFs with sections on background, objective, audience, tone of voice, and mandatories.

Generate an editable Google Doc until the user stops the generation

Step 2.step_action: Brainstorm with Claude to turn the brief into three named visual territories, each with a keyword set and a rationale. I gather and edit reference imagery and assemble the three moodboards in Figma, batch-correcting the references so each board reads as one coherent world. I then ask Claude to pressure-test each territory against the brief and tell me which is weakest.

nodes.label: Request three visual territories from Claude
nodes.detail: Attaching their edited brief, the user asks Claude to help develop three distinct visual territories, each with its own keyword set and rationale, and explicitly instructs Claude not to recommend a favorite since that choice should be theirs.

nodes.label: Read edited brief first and ask clarification question
Answer clarifying questions
Deliver three named territories with rationale
nodes.detail: Claude returns three named visual territories, each with palette, rationale and risk notes: '01 El taller' (the workshop; annotation, chalk marks, spec tickets), '02 Viento del este' (the weather it was built for; grey light, salt haze, horizon lines), and '03 Cuarenta anos' (forty years; heritage as durability evidence, a fifteen-year-old jacket as record). It builds a presentation document laying out all three plus a comparison table.

nodes.label: Build moodboard for El taller in Figma
nodes.detail: The user judges all three territories good and likes 'El taller' most because they can already picture its visual universe. They open Figma, sources reference images from Pinterest (workshop scenes, thread spools, chalk marks, deadstock fabric), and assembles them into a moodboard while defining a cream/gray/charcoal/rust palette given the client's preference for black and white.

nodes.detail: In a second Figma frame they deliberately search for genuinely bad Atlantic weather photography of the brand's home city rather than typical leisure/surf imagery, aiming to argue the jacket withstands harsh coastal conditions rather than reading as a summer souvenir.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to pressure-test the two moodboards
nodes.detail: Back in the Claude desktop app, the user shares the Figma boards and asks Claude to pressure-test each of them against the original brief and tell them which is the weakest.

nodes.label: Report inability to view Figma link and state test criteria
nodes.detail: Claude reports it cannot see the Figma link content directly (needs the Chrome extension or an authorized Figma connector it cannot run here) and declines to critique boards it hasn't actually looked at. It states the criteria it will test against once images are provided: hard gates, territory integrity, and proposition proof, plus a prior expectation that Viento del este will be the weaker board.

nodes.label: Send screenshots of both moodboards
nodes.detail: The user exports and sends screenshot images of both moodboards directly in the chat, labeling the top image as territory 1 (El taller) and the bottom image as territory 2 (Viento del este).

nodes.detail: Contrary to its own prior expectation, Claude concludes El taller (territory 1, the workshop board) is the weaker of the two: it flags a 'surf-brand disqualifier' image, calls the board 'not specific to anything' (could be a craft studio in Brooklyn, Copenhagen or Melbourne), and notes the casting skews younger than the brand's actual makers. It calls Viento del este verifiably local and a real asset, though it flags a risk that the board reads as coastal melancholy rather than weather-as-adversary.

nodes.label: Disagree with parts of the critique and proceed with El taller

They decide to continue refining territory one (El taller) regardless of Claude's weaker-board verdict.

Step 3.step_action: I design different logo routes in Illustrator for the two strongest territories. I describe each route to Claude (and share exports) and ask for a critique on legibility, memorability and ownability, plus a list of similarity risks I should check before showing the client. I then refine each route into full lockups.

nodes.label: Sketch six wordmark variations in Illustrator
nodes.detail: In the spirit of time, the user drafts logo ideas directly in Illustrator rather than by hand, sketching six 'LONG WAY' wordmark variations in a grid — mixing bold sans caps, brush script, and handwritten cursive styles aimed at crafts/handmade positioning.

nodes.label: Pick a favorite wordmark before checking with Claude
nodes.detail: They narrow to a favorite version among the six drafted wordmarks, planning to check whether Claude agrees before finalizing, and prepares to screenshot their selections.

nodes.label: Attempt to share screenshot as Claude desktop app crashes
nodes.detail: While trying to attach a screenshot of the six wordmark variations to the Claude desktop app, the app fails to attach the image, then stops responding entirely ('It has stopped working'), forcing them to force-quit and restart it.

nodes.label: Recover by creating a Claude Project and a fresh chat
nodes.detail: After the crash and restart, the user protects their prior audit chat by adding it to a new 'Long Way' Claude Project, then starts a brand-new chat named 'Territory 1 logo critique' inside that project.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to critique their logos
nodes.detail: They upload the wordmark screenshot and requests a critique on legibility, memorability and ownability, plus a list of similarity risks to check before showing the client.

nodes.label: Ask basic brand questions due to lost context
nodes.detail: Because the new chat has none of the detailed context from the earlier crashed session, Claude first has to ask fundamental clarifying questions before it can help: 'What is Long Way — what does the brand actually sell or do?' (offering options like travel/outdoors, food & drink, apparel/lifestyle) and 'Where will the logo have to work hardest?' (digital, packaging, apparel, or broad). This is a clear instance of AI-collaboration friction caused by the crash losing prior session memory.

nodes.label: Answer clarifying questions
nodes.detail: The user answers Claude's re-grounding questions, remarking on camera that Claude 'has forgot what we discussed on the previous chat.'.

nodes.label: Deliver wordmark critique and similarity-risk list
nodes.detail: Claude completes its critique of the six drafted wordmark variations, scoring each on legibility, memorability, and ownability, and gives per-option verdicts (e.g. #2 as the clear top pick, #3 as worth keeping only for secondary packaging, #5 as most energetic but least distinctive). It lists similarity risks including a name conflict with the established 'Long Way Round' travel/adventure brand, font-licensing exposure for options set in retail display fonts rather than redrawn from scratch, and genre-saturation risk versus surf/skate competitors.

nodes.label: Build typography-pairing mockups
nodes.detail: While Claude works, they continue in Illustrator building typography-pairing mockups, testing several headline/subtitle/body font combinations (e.g. Bodoni, SignPainter/HouseScript) against sample layout text.

nodes.label: Disagree with Claude's top recommendation as recording ends
nodes.detail: The user reviews Claude's pick on camera and says they disagree with it, explaining that Claude's notes on the recommended option effectively argue for switching creative direction entirely (toward a more condensed, competitor-adjacent look), which they are not willing to do. The recording ends here, mid-work.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: Source is 3e because that's when the user succeeds in sending a clear task prompt to claude post crash. Target is 3h because that's the output the user is responding to and deciding to reject here.

Step 1.output: creative_brief.docx containing the audit findings, a competitor matrix, a positioning statement and three proposed strategic directions
Step 1.tools: Free version: Figma (Starter), Google Docs, Paid version: Claude Max, Adobe Illustrator (Creative Cloud All Apps)
rubrics: The audit names at least 5 specific, concrete weaknesses in the current identity rather than generic design advice
The competitor matrix covers at least 5 real competitors, each with positioning and visual language described
The brief contains all required sections: objective, audience, tone of voice, mandatories, success criteria
The three strategic directions are meaningfully distinct, not three phrasings of the same idea
No invented facts about the client or its competitors; anything uncertain is explicitly flagged as an assumption

ratings.output_quality_reason: It gave me a comprehensive analysis of the market, but didn’t provide me with 5 competitors nor with a competitor matrix.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The AI provided a broad market analysis, with helpful insights and correctly sourced information.

I gather and edit reference imagery and assemble the three moodboards in Figma, batch-correcting the references so each board reads as one coherent world. I then ask Claude to pressure-test each territory against the brief and tell me which is weakest.
Step 2.output: moodboards.fig (3 boards) and territory_rationales.md with a name, keyword set and one-paragraph rationale per territory
Step 2.tools: Free version: Figma (Starter), Unsplash. Paid version: Claude Max, Adobe Photoshop (Creative Cloud All Apps)
rubrics: Each of the three territories has a distinct name, keyword set and one paragraph rationale
Every rationale traces back to a specific line or claim in the creative brief
The territories differ on at least two axes (e.g. color temperature, typographic voice, imagery style)
At least one territory is a genuine creative risk rather than a safe default
The critique names which territory is weakest and explains why in terms of the brief

ratings.output_quality_reason: It provided me with three distinctive directions, but one of them wasn’t viable.
